# In Praise of the Index

There is a person who read the book you're holding more carefully than you ever will, and you almost certainly don't know their name.

I mean the indexer. Most nonfiction books of any heft end with a few dense pages of alphabetized terms and numbers, and most readers treat those pages the way they treat the copyright notice: as furniture. But an index is not generated. Even now, good ones are mostly made by hand, by people who read a manuscript line by line and ask, over and over, *what is this passage actually about, and what would someone be looking for when they need it?*

That second question is the hard one. A concordance, which lists every place a word appears, is easy; a machine can do it in a blink. But an index is a map of *meaning*, not of vocabulary. If a biography spends three pages on its subject's grief after a sibling's death without once using the word "grief," a concordance will miss it entirely. An indexer won't. They'll write "grief, over brother's death, 112–15," and in doing so they'll make an interpretive claim about what those pages contain. Every entry is a tiny act of literary criticism.

I love the small decisions involved. Should it be "Lincoln, Abraham, assassination of" or "assassination, of Lincoln"? Probably both, with one pointing to the other. That's what the humble *see also* is for: it admits that people come at the same idea from different doors. And the difference between *see* and *see also* is quietly profound. *See* means "we filed it over there; you're in the wrong place, but that's fine." *See also* means "you're in the right place, and there's more." One is a redirection, the other an invitation.

Indexers have their own sly traditions. There's a long, half-joking history of indexes that editorialize. One often-told example is an entry along the lines of "Macaulay, Thomas Babington, his inaccuracy, 12, 45, 78..." inserted by someone who clearly had opinions. Lewis Carroll indexed one of his own books with entries that were small jokes. The index, it turns out, is a place where a careful reader can leave fingerprints.

What moves me about all this is that the index is built entirely for a future stranger in a hurry. Nobody reads an index for pleasure. You come to it with a need: *where did she talk about the drought?* The indexer has anticipated you. Months or years earlier, they imagined someone standing in a library or sitting up late, half-remembering a passage, and they laid down a path to it. It's a kind of care that only shows up when it's needed, and otherwise disappears completely.

There's a whole category of work like this, work whose success is measured by its invisibility. Copyeditors whose best fixes you never notice. Typographers whose choices you feel but can't name. The engineer who made the elevator ride so smooth you forgot you were moving. We tend to celebrate the visible gesture, the author on the cover, the architect at the ribbon-cutting. But a lot of the texture of a livable world comes from people who asked, patiently and without applause, *what will someone need here, later, when I'm not around to help?*

Search has made indexes feel old-fashioned, and for many purposes it's genuinely better. You can find any string of characters instantly. But search finds what you typed, not what you meant. It can't tell you that the passage you're thinking of never uses the word you remember. It can't offer you a *see also*. It doesn't read the book first.

So the next time you flip to the back of a thick book, spend a moment there. Look at how the entries are broken down, which subtopics got their own lines, what got cross-referenced to what. You're looking at one person's patient understanding of the whole, folded into a few pages so you could find your way in.

It's a strange and generous thing: a map drawn by someone who walked every inch of the territory, handed to you so you'd never have to.
